full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarker, J: This is an application under section 228 read with section 229 of the Companies Act, 1994 (briefly, the Companies Act) at the instance of Bangladesh Steel Re-Rolling. Mills Limited, being the transferee-company, and BSRM Steel Mills Limited, being the transferor-company, seeking approval of a scheme of amalgamation of the above two companies, whereby the entire undertaking of the transferor-company, as going concerns together with all assets and liabilities, are proposed to be transferred to and vested in the transferee-company.

2. The petitioner No. 1 Bangladesh Steel Re-Rolling Mills Limited (transferee-company) was incorporated as a private company under the Companies Act, 1913 (since repealed and substituted by the Companies Act, 1994) in the year 1960 in Chattogram with the objects, inter alia, to carry on the business of steel rolling and re-rolling mills for manufacturing MS products such as MS rods, rounds, flats, squares, wire rods, MS angles, tees, channels and other sections, bolts & nuts, wires etc and, thereafter, having been converted into a public limited company on 03 November, 2009, it started trading of the shares of the company in Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) and Chittagong Stock' Exchange (CSE) from 27 April, 2015. It is stated that the transferee-company is one of the oldest and largest producers of structural steel in Bangladesh, which has an authorized share capital of Taka 500,00,00.000 only divided into 50,00,00,000 ordinary shares of Taka I0 each and the issued, subscribed and paid-up capital is Taka 236,06,82,360 divided into 23,60,68,236 shares of Taka 10 each. 3. The petitioner No. 2 BSRM Steel Mills Limited (transferor-company) initially was incorporated as a private limited company under the Companies Act with: registration No. CH-6561(267) of 2008 with the objects, inter ,alia, to supply billets to its sister concerns, including the transferee-company which are involved in producing high grade MS rod, angle, channel etc and later was converted into a public company. It is stated that :the transferor-company is an automatic steel melting plant and produces high-quality 'MS Billet' for steel re-rolling mills and is considered to be one of the world's largest Induction furnace based melting plant. The transferor-company has an authorized share capital of Taka 600,00,00,000 only divided into 60,00,00,000 ordinary shares of Taka 10 each and the issued, subscribed and paid-up capital is Taka 394,43,54,000 divided into 39,44,35,400 shares of Taka 10 each. 5. It is stated that the transferor-company is a subsidiary of the transferee-company and clause II1(m) of the object clause in Memorandum of Association (MoA) of the transferee company permits amalgamation with the transferor company; likewise, clause 111(23) of the object clause in MoA of the transferor company permits this .amalgamation. It is stated that the process of steel making justifies amalgamation of a final product manufacturer (the transferee company) with a backward-linkage/raw material manufacturer (the transferor company), because in the steel production process, recycled materials as well as traditional raw materials, such as iron, rods, coal, and limestone are melted and heated to produce high quality molten steel billets (MS Billets) and these billets are treated in the next step by adding or removing certain elements and/or manipulating the temperature and production environment. The MS Billets are used as raw materials for the manufacture of structural products, such as rods, angle and bars through a process called re-rolling. As the transferor-company is engaged in production of MS Billets and the transferee-company is engaged in the process of re-rolling to make the final product for sale to consumers, the amalgamation would pave the way for general consumers, dealers and suppliers of steel products to obtain a 'one-stop solution' from a single entity to meet up their need of steel products. In an expectation of increasing profitability, by creating a combined entity, the Board of Directors of the transferee company resolved in the board meeting dated 16th September, 2016 that the companies be amalgamated, and the Board of Directors of the transferor company resolved in the board meeting dated 16th September, 2016 that the companies be amalgamated. Hence, this application.

6. By filing an affidavit-in-opposition and a supplementary thereto, the respondent No. 2-Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC) states, amongst other, that the proposed scheme of amalgamation should not be sanctioned due to the reasons that general shareholders will be losers as (i) the transferor company has huge liability compared to low net asset, (ii) the Net Asset Value (NAV) was considered at revaluation price rather than historical cost and (iii) the retained earnings of the transferor company was negative until 30-6-2018, in other words, the transferor company has huge liabilities. It is stated that the asset of the transferor company has been revalued by ACNABIN Chartered Accountants Firm and the petitioner-companies with malafide intention have managed the report in question as prepared by ACNABIN CA firm using tactics and without following international accounting standards to hide actual financial position of the companies, because it is evident from the audited financial statements of BSRM Steel Mills Limited as on 30-6-2019 that the transferor company incurred accumulated loss of Taka 7.25 crore as on 30-6-2018 whereas the earning based valuation of share price has been determined 34.96 per share considering 2 (two) years only which asserts ill motive of the petitioners and further, while the plant of the transferor company normally manufactures 8,62,500 Metric Ton products, in 2019 the volume of its production capacity has been shown 9,13,241 Metric Ton which is 106% of its total capacity i.e. the value of share of the transferor company has been shown to be augmented dramatically. It is stated that acceptance of that report of ACNABIN is disputed to BSEC on identical issue; on 28-1-2020, the BSEC raised objection against this firm and advised Institute of Chartered Accountants of Bangladesh (ICAB) to take legal action against them and the same information has been reported in the Financial Express on 30-1-2020 and 22-8-2020, in the New Age on 29-1-2020 and 23-8-2020 and in the Business Standard on 30-1-2020 and 23-8-2020). It is stated that the fate of the general investors shall be like that of the Keya Cosmetics Ltd which was amalgamated with private company in the manner as proposed here in this case.

7. Mr Tanjub-ul Alam, the learned Advocates appearing for the petitioners, at the very outset having presented an overview of the case, seeks this Court's permission to make detailed submission by his junior Mr lmran Anwar. Mr lmran Anwar then, takes this Court through the various clauses of the scheme of amalgamation in an endeavour to place the modus operandi of the proposed amalgamation, and contends that through the scheme of amalgamation of the transferor-company with the transferee-company, the entire undertaking of the transferor-company as a going concern, together with all its assets and liabilities relating thereto. have been proposed to be transferred to and vested in the transferee-company; that the assets, licenses, permits and other benefits and privileges held by or conferred upon the transferor-company will be vested in the transferee-company without any further act, instrument or deed, pursuant to clause 7 of the scheme; that all liabilities of the transferor-company shall likewise be vested in the transferee-company without any further act, instrument or deed, pursuant to clause 8 of the scheme.

8. Regarding valuation of these two companies, Mr Anwar contends that the transferor-company is a non-listed company and, as such, there is no published market price for the shares; that in undertaking this task, the valuer considered historical information to determine Net Asset Value (NAV) method of valuation and Earning Based Valuation (EBV) method of valuation; that historical financial information was collected from the audited financial statements of the companies and market information was collected from official website of Dhaka Stock Exchange and published report/ reviews of Dhaka Stock Exchange Limited; that applying the usual methodology, the NAV per share was deduced at Taka 34.57 based on the audited financial statements as of 30 June, 2019 in respect of the transferor-company; that in determining the Earning Per Share in respect of the transferor-company, the net profit after tax was considered for the years 2017-18 and 2018-19, being the data of last two years since the company maintained operation at desired capacity; that from the calculation done by the ACNABIN, the EBV per share stands at Taka 34.96 in respect of the transferor-company; that taking an average, the value per share has been calculated as Taka 34.76 for the transferor-company. On the other hand, he continues to submit, the transferee-company is a listed entity, its shares' market price of each day is available from DSE; that as appears in the report, the transferee-company has a NAV per share at Taka 97.46 in consideration of the audited financial statements as of 30 June, 2019; that under the EBV method, the audited financial statements of the transferee-company since 2014-15 up until 2018-19 was considered, i.e. for a period of five years, and the average P/E ratio for 6 months starting from 31-01-2019 until 30-06-2019 as available from the Dhaka Stock Exchange was taken into consideration; that applying this methodology, EBV per share for the transferee-company stood at Taka 41.44; that on average of the prices calculated under NAV and EBV method, the value for each share in the transferee-company stood at Taka 69.45 and, accordingly, for the purpose of merger, the share exchange ratio was set at 1:0.5005.

9. In an effort to detail the share exchange ratio and distribution of shares among the shareholders of the transferor company, Mr Imran Anwar submits that the method to be applied for reorganization of capital of these two companies is that the transferee-company shall issue and allot the ordinary shares of Taka 10 in the ratio of 0.5005 (zero point five zero zero five) ordinary shares in the transferee-company for every 1 (one) ordinary share of the face value of Taka 10 held in the transferor-company to the ordinary shareholders of the transferor company whose names are recorded in the register of members on a date to be fixed by the Board of Directors of the transferee-company, which would be the "Record Date"; that these newly issued shares of the transferee-company shall be issued, allotted and credited as fully paid up in favour of the shareholders of the transferor-company; that the transferee-company would issue 10,86,43,936 ordinary shares of Taka 10 each to the shareholders of the transferor-company as consideration towards the settlement of this transaction as per the scheme. In an endeavour to rebut the allegation of inflation in the value of the transferor company's assets by revaluation, Mr Anwar places before this Court the various provisions of the International Standard on Auditing (ISA) and International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), and submits that all companies are permitted to revalue their assets within an interval of three to five years and since the last valuation was done in 2011 for Bangladesh Steel Re-rolling Mills Limited and in 2012 for BSRM Steel Mills Limited, there is no bar on revaluation in 2019 as per international accounting standards. Then, he claims that if revaluation were not done, more shares were required to be issued from the transferee entity to the shareholders of the transferor company inasmuch as in the proposed exchange ratio of 1:0.5005, the transferee company is required to issue 108,643,936 shares, whereas without revaluation the share exchange ratio stands at 1:0.513688 and the transferee company is required to issue 111,506,614 under the old valuation, resulting into 2,862,679 additional shares to be issued by the transferee company.

10. With regard to the issue of having Negative Retained Earnings of the transferor company, Mr Imran Anwar submits that negative retained earnings are not bar to amalgamation under any law, because a company may have negative retained earnings for a variety of reasons and the companies usually have negative retained earnings in initial years of operation, as is the case for transferor company up to 30-6-2018 because during early years of operation the company needs to make investment more than its income, and generation of income gradually increases over the period. By taking me through Paragraphs 39-42 of the International Accounting Standard (IAS)-16, Mr Anwar submits that revaluation of asset does not increase retained earnings, rather revaluation is recorded under a separate head, namely, revaluation reserve. He contends that the retained earnings has already became positive for the transferor company as the transferor company started to make profits since 2018 and, currently, it has a solid positive retained earnings after two consecutive years of profit and, as of today, remains as a financially healthy company. On the other hand, Mr Anwar adds, the retained earnings of transferee company as of 30 June 2019 is over 795 crore BDT as of 30th June 2019. He contends that while the transferor company has liability of 3,199 crore BDT as of 30 June 2019, it has more asset of 4,563 crore BDT as of 30 June 2019 and, in case of transferee company for the year ending on 30 June 2019, the total asset of transferee is Taka 5,255 crores and total liability is Taka 2954 crores. In the consolidated financial statement for the year ended 30 June, 2019, upon consolidation, the total asset is Taka 91,067,184,337 and the total liabilities is Taka 60,558,665,062 and, therefore, the transferor company is a profitable concern and the amalgamation is going to happen between two financially solvent and sound companies.

11. Regarding compliance of the relevant laws, Rules and this Court's Directions/Orders, Mr Anwar contends that following the meeting of the Board of Directors of the transferee company, which is a listed entity, it duly declared Price Sensitive Information ("PSI") through the Dhaka and Chittagong Stock Exchanges and published the PSI on 17-9-2019 in two newspapers as per the applicable rules framed by the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission, namely, Dhaka Stock Exchange (Listing) Regulations, 2015 and সিকিউরিটিজ ও এক্সচেন্জ কমিশন (সুবিধাভোগী ব্যবসা নিষিদ্ধকরণ), বিধিমালা, ১৯৯৫; that upon preliminary Court Order on 14-10-2019, the respective companies published another PSI through Dhaka and Chittagong Stock Exchanges and published the PSI on 22-10-2019 in two newspapers as per the applicable rules framed by the Bangladesh Securities and. Exchange Commission, namely, Dhaka Stock Exchange (Listing) Regulations, 2015 and সিকিউরিটিজ ও এক্সচেন্জ কমিশন (সুবিধাভোগী ব্যবসা নিষিদ্ধকরণ), বিধিমালা, ১৯৯৫। He contends that the petitioners also have fully complied with the Order dated 14-10-2019 of this Court, such as, the transferee company called an EGM by issuing notice dated 23-10-2019, the said notice was communicated to the shareholders of the transferee company by exhausting various mechanisms to ensure maximum participation; that the shareholders of the transferee company in the EGM dated 18-12-2019 unanimously approved the scheme of amalgamation; that out of the total shareholders, 504 shareholders were present in the meeting and none of the shareholders raises any objection regarding the amalgamation and since the shareholders present unanimously voted for a special resolution, the scheme of amalgamation was duly approved; that in similar way, upon duly issuance of notice to the shareholders of the transferor company, its EGM was held on 18-12-2019 that the shareholders attending the EGM unanimously passed a special resolution to approve the scheme of amalgamation. Mr Anwar further contends that according to the Order of this Court, all the creditors of the transferee company were notified for the creditors meeting on 21-11-2019 through registered-post notice dated 29-10-2019; that the resolution was passed unanimously by all the creditors who represent 90% in terms of value of liabilities of the transferee company and, in the same manner, all the creditors of the transferor company were notified for the creditors' meeting on 21-11-2019 through registered post notice dated 29-10-2019; that the resolution was passed unanimously by all the creditors present, who in aggregate represent 90% in terms of value of liabilities of the transferee, and none of the creditors of either company raised any objection against the amalgamation till today.

12. With regard to allegation against the ACNABIN, Mr lmran Anwar contends that there is an allegation against a partner of ACNABIN named Mr Rokunuzzaman, FCA in relation to their work for Aman Feed Limited, which has nothing to do with the present case, because the partner involved in this case is Mr Mominul Karim FCA. He contends that the allegation raised by the BSEC on this score is contrary to established legal maxim of "presumption of innocence until proven guilty" and, more importantly, ACNABIN is listed as a recognized accounting firm both by the BSEC and Bangladesh Bank, and just because there is allegation against one of their partners does not invalidate their work or their credibility, particularly when a different partner, as in this present case, carries out the work. Mr lmran Anwar, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, argues that there have been numerous communications between the petitioner companies and the BSEC regarding this merger and, in none of these occasions, the BSEC raised any issue of objection relating to the amalgamation, nor did it issue any letter of objection to the transferee company or the transferor company. He contends that ACNABIN being not disqualified from carrying out the audit work or valuation work by any Court in Bangladesh or by any regulatory authority and, in the absence of such disqualification, ACNABIN's report should not be questioned inasmuch as that would render all work of ACNABIN invalid, questionable and dubious since the point of time when the allegation was raised; that the petitioners engaged ACNABIN because it is a widely reputed chartered accountant firm who has considerable experience in carrying out audit and valuation work; that the valuation was carried out much earlier compared to the point in time when the allegation against ACNABIN was raised and the allegation relating to Aman Feed has no connection with regard to the valuation in the present case so as to render their entire work unreliable. Mr Imran Anwar submits that there is no illegality in the valuation process, as not a single one that the respondent BSEC has been able to point out, nor has there been any violation or non-compliance of legal provision in carrying out the valuation exercise and so there is no justification to appoint an audit firm adding costs and complexity to the process of amalgamation. He submits that there is no requirement under law for appointment of valuation expert in the given scenario where a valuation has already been conducted by an independent audit firm having enlistment with the BSEC and the Bangladesh Bank. He claims that this petition is completely a bona fide one.

13. He then prays that since all the requirements of section 228(2) of the Companies Act have been clearly satisfied, this Court should allow this petition.

14. Per contra Mr AM Masum, the learned Advocate for the BSEC, submits that the proposed scheme of amalgamation is inaccurate and unfair inasmuch as the assets of the transferor company have been revalued from around Taka 323 crore to Taka 978 crore which is 3 times of actual value, whereas, the assets of the transferee company have not been revalued and consequently it impacts upon the calculation of NAV, EPS, EBV, PIE etc and thereby the price of the share of transferor company has been shown to be increased which is totally incongruous with accounting policy and practice. By taking me through the provisions of Rules 3(3)(a) and 14(d) of the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (Public Issue) Rules, 2015, the learned Advocate for the BSEC strenuously submits that the petitioner-companies have prepared the scheme of amalgamation in violation of the aforesaid laws. He submits that ERRS-13 (Fair Value Measurement) prescribes three widely used valuation techniques which are (i) market approach, (ii) the cost approach and (iii) the income approach, and single valuation technique may be applied in case of quoted price in active market, otherwise multiple valuation techniques shall be apt and evaluated considering the reasonableness of the range of values indicated by those result, but ACNABIN has prepared the audit report without following the said principles of accounting.

15. In a bid to place before this Court his concerns about the interest and right of the general shareholders, Mr Masum, the learned Advocate for the BSEC, submits that as per the scheme of amalgamation, the net asset value of the transferee company is Taka 2,300 crore against its debt worth of Taka 1,527 crore and hence, the debt is 33.61 percent lower than net asset but after merger, this debt would be about 15.11 percent more than its net asset value which consequently will be shifted upon shoulder of its general investor. He submits that in the report prepared by ACNABIN Chartered Accountants Firm, 5 years weighted average earning per share has been considered for the transferee company's share valuation and its EPS is shown as 6.7438 whereas EPS has been shown as 2.6800 for the transferor company by taking into only 2 years weighted average earning per share and, furthermore, only the transferee company's market price earnings ratio (P/E-6.10) has been considered for the transferee company's share valuation whereas summation of 4 peers has been considered in case of the transferor company which inflated share price and exchange ratio of the transferor company abnormally and in case of transfer of shares and repatriation of sale proceeds of shares in favor of non-listed company, fair value of the shares shall be determined by weighted average calculation of all the 3 (three) valuation approaches i.e. NAV, market value and discounted cash flow approach, but only one method of valuation and exchange ratio has been used by ACNABIN Chartered Accountants Firm in proposed amalgamation which is not justified.

16. He submits that from the audited financial statements of both the companies as on 30-6-2019, it is apparent that the transferor company is high geared company having total bank liabilities of Taka 2,788 crore whereas the transferee company is a lower risky company having total bank liabilities of Taka 1,527.75 crore and therefore after amalgamation, unquoted shares of the transferor company shall be liquidated in a publically listed company by exchanging quoted shares of publicly listed company; and since 59.06% share belongs to general investors, burden of this colossal amount of aforesaid loan will go upon the public shareholders and, as such, the merger of these companies should not be allowed. He submits that following the merger of these two companies, the public shareholder will be loser in that the transferor company is going to transfer net asset amounting to Taka 541.51 crore against 1,86,43,936 number of shares of the transferee company and the market value of these share is only Taka 544.30 crore at Taka 50.10 per share as on 21st January, 2020 which is the lowest price over last two years, albeit the market price per share on 30th June, 2019 was Taka 70.90. He further submits that the transferor company has progressed its commercial operation from l6thJune, 2016 until 2019 and its asset has been revalued by Taka 822.06 crore from historical book value of Taka 1,631.06 crore as on 30-6-2019 which is at 50.37% by 3 years and therefore general investors holding 59.06% shares will be losers if the proposed scheme of amalgamation is allowed and as the proposed scheme of amalgamation is tactics of the sponsor-directors of the transferor company to reduce burden of its debt by placing the same upon investors of the transferee company since Net Asset of the transferor company has been estimated at Taka 1,363 crore and the liability of this company is Taka x,788 crore and therefore NAV of the transferor company is about 51 percent less than aforesaid debt and debt of the transferee company will increase by more than 280 percent and, as such, the general investors will be losers for fusion of companies.

17. The learned Advocate for the BSEC submits that since there is no specific Rules and Regulations for conducting amalgamation in our country, some opportunists, like the petitioners-companies, with malafide intention use tactics to avail facility of liquidity of shares under sections 228 and 229 of the Companies Act in the alternative way of scheme of amalgamation and consequently the general investors fall in loss: He then submits that from the scheme of amalgamation, it is evident that the transferee company holds 23,60,68,237 shares whereas the transferor company holds 39,44,35,400 shares and the new allotted shares will be 10,86,43.936 by the exchange ratio of 1:0.500 and therefore transferee company will hold total (23,60,68,237 + 10,86,43,936) = 34,47,12,172 shares after merger, out of which the sponsor shareholders will hold 76.09% shares, which are 26,22,91,491.67 in number, and pursuant to Commission's Notification No. SEC/CM RRCD/ 2009-193/119/Admin/34 dated November 22, 2011, the sponsor shareholders of the transferee company will be eligible to sell 46.09% (76.09-30%) which is 12,08,90,148.28 shares in number, in the regular market for which prevailing market share price will be diluted significantly.

18. He refers to the cases of Kay and Que (BD) Ltd vs Registrar, Joint Stock Co. as cited in 2019(2) LNJ 124 and submits that a Court of law is competent to examine the just and fair aspect of a remedy sought for by the petitioner in course of dealing with any type of case and submits that this Court is required to consider the pros and cons of the scheme to see whether the scheme is in favour of the public interest. By referring to the case of PHP NOF Continuous Galvanizing Mills Ltd vs PHP Steels Ltd., 19 MLR 374 and (1994) 3 Comp LI 46 (Born), Mr AM Masum submits that the Court may disturb the scheme if the valuation arrived at is grossly unfair and not justifiable considering the valuation report conducted by independent, impartial and qualified chartered accountant, and argues that the proposed fusion of the petitioners' companies fall within the purview of this well-settled principle and envisioned to create monopoly, disturb competitive environ-ment in the Cap Market and seriously affect interest of public shareholders-investors.

19. By summing up his all the contentions and submissions made hereinbefore, he submits that it is crystal clear that the proposed merger is manifestly illegal and malafide as it is designed for evading security laws, policy and guidelines of the BSEC and is intended to swindle the money from public shareholders/investors and, as such, this application for approval of the proposed scheme of amalgamation should be rejected for ends of justice and public interest. He submits that the instant respondent is the regulator of the securities and also is the representative of the general shareholders in that the provision of section 8 of Act, 1993 bestowed the pivotal statutory duty upon BSEC to protect the public interest, and since the provision of section 229(1) of the Companies Act empowered Company Court to pass any kind of Order, including consequential Order, the proposed scheme should not only be dismissed, but exemplary costs should be slapped.

20. After hearing the learned Advocates, perusing the petition and affidavits-in-opposition together with their annexures and reading the relevant statutory laws plus case-laws, it appears to this. Court that the issues to be adjudicated upon by this Court are; (i) whether the petitioner companies' instant application satisfies the legal requirements under section 228 of the Companies Act, (ii) whether the petitioner companies violated any laws of the land in preparation of the scheme of amalgamation, (iii) whether the petitioner companies' audit reports were prepared in consonance with the provisions/Guidelines of the International Accounting Standard (IAS), (iv) whether the interests of the general shareholders i.e. the public interest would be jeopardized in any manner because of the proposed amalgamation, (v) whether this Court is competent to interfere with the audit report prepared by the petitioner-companies CA Firm for the purpose of amalgamation and (vi) if this Court decides to okay the proposed scheme of the amalgamation, then, what provisions should be made by this Court under section 229 of the Companies Act.

21. For an effective adjudication of the issue No. 1, namely, whether the petitioner-companies' instant application satisfies the legal requirements under sections 228 & 229 of the Companies Act, it would be useful to be acquainted with the provisions of sections 228 and 229 of the Companies Act, which are reproduced below:

Section 228: Power to compromise with creditors and members:—

(1) Where a compromise or arrangement is proposed between a company and its creditors or any class of them, or between the company and its members or any class of them, the Court may, on the application in summary way of the company or of any creditor or member of the company or, in the case of a company being wound up, of the liquidator, order a meeting of the creditors or class of creditors, or the members of the company or class of members, as the case may be, to be called held and conducted in such manner as the Court directs.

(2) If a majority in number representing three-fourths in value of creditors, or of members as the case may be, present either in person or by proxy at the meeting, agree to any compromise or arrangement, the compromise or arrangement shall if sanctioned by the Court be binding on all the creditors or the class of creditors, on all the members or class of members, as the case may be, and also on the company, in the case of a company in the course of being wound up, on the liquidator and contributories of the company.

(3)     ………………..

(4)      ………………..

(5)      ………………..

(6)      ………………..

(7)   ………………..

22. From a plain reading of the above-quoted law, it appears to this Court that pursuant to making any arrangement by a company with another company or by the members/creditors of a company with the company, whenever any of them approaches this Court, it may direct the members/creditors/company to call, hold and conduct a meeting in an appropriate manner. And, if the said meeting is attended by majority in number, i.e. by more than fifty percent, of the members/creditors who holds three-fourths shares/credits in value and agree to the proposed arrangement, it shall be binding upon all the concerned, subject to obtaining sanction from this Court.

23. Section 229: Provisions for facilitating arrangements, and compromises:—

(l) Where an application is made to the Court under section 228 for the sanctioning of a compromise or arrangement proposes between a company and any such persons as are mentioned in that section, and it is shown to the Court that the compromise or arrangement has been proposed for the purposes of, or in connection with, a scheme for the reconstruction of any company or companies to the amalgamation of any two or more companies, and that under the scheme the whole or any part of the undertaking and the property of any company concerned in the scheme, in this section referred to as a transferor company, is to be transferred to another company in this section referred to as the transferee company, the Court may, either by the order sanctioning the compromise or arrangement or by any subsequent order, make provision for all or any of the following matters:—

(a) the transfer to the transferee company of the whole or any part of the undertaking and of the property or liabilities of any transferor company;

(b) the allotting or appropriation by the transferee company of any shares, debentures, policies, or other like interests in that company which under the compromise or arrangement are to be allotted or appropriate by that company to or for any person;

(c) the continuation by or against the transferee company of any legal proceedings pending by or against any transferor company;

(d) the dissolution, without winding up, of any transferor company;

(e) the provision to be made for any person who, within such time and in such manner as the Court directs, dissents from the compromise or arrangement; such incidental, consequential and supplemental matters as are necessary to secure that the reconstruction or amalgamation shall be fully and effectively carried out.

(2) Where an order under this section provides for the transfer of property or liabilities, that property shall by virtue of the order, be transferred to and vest in, and those liabilities shall by virtue of the order transferred to and become the liabilities of the transferee company, and in the case of any property, if the order so directs, it shall be freed from any charge which is, by virtue of the compromise or arrangement to cease to have effect.

(3)   ………………..

(4)   ………………..

(5)      ………………..

24. From a simple reading of the provisions of section 229 of the Companies Act all that 1 understand is that when a petition for sanctioning of an scheme of amalgamation is presented before this Court invoking section 228 of the Companies Act, section 229 of the Companies Act empowers this Court to pass necessary incidental, consequential and supplemental Orders and/or Directions, including but not restricted to, (i) transferring of the undertaking, and of the properties /liabilities of the transferor company to the transferee company, (ii) allotment/ appropriation of shares, debentures, policies and other interest by the transferee company, (iii) taking the liability of the legal proceedings of the transferor company, either by continuing with the same or settling it, either at the time of sanctioning the scheme or at any time subsequent thereto, upon exercising the Court's discretionary power.

25. Now, let me see whether the petitioner-companies have been compliant to the provisions of section 228 of the companies towards enabling this Court to pass appropriate Orders/Directions under section 229 of the Companies Act.

26. From the annexed papers, it appears to this Court that the members of the transferor company have made an arrangement with the members of the transferee company to get merged into one company and the ultimate surviving company shall be the transferee company. Accordingly, both the companies approached this Court for obtaining this Court's nod thereto. Upon admission of the matter on 14-10-2019, the petitioner- companies were directed to display their resolutions as to getting amalgamation in the screen/news portals of the DSE and CSE and, also, in the two daily national newspapers by inviting all the shareholders and creditors to attend the meeting. It is to be clarified here that when a. meeting under section 228 of the Companies Act is called, held and conducted at the instance of the Company Court, the said meeting should be treated as a mere general meeting, though it is popularly called and recorded by the Courts, Company Secretaries and other concerns as the Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM); because calling, holding and conducting an EGM, as provided in section 84 of the Companies Act, are different from that of a meeting under section 228 of the Companies Act. But a meeting called and held by a company and/or its shareholders and/or its creditors for making any arrangement under section 228 of the Companies Act before approaching the Company Court, is to be recorded as EGM. From the annexed papers, it is evident that the petitioner-companies accordingly exhibited their scheme in the news portals and websites of the. DSE and CSE and also published the same in two daily newspapers. Thereafter, affidavit-in-compliance was duly filed on 04-11-2019, as evident from annexures L-series. The petitioner-companies also have held their respective meetings for approval of the scheme of amalgamation on 18-12-2019, as evidenced by annexures U & V-1. It transpires from the minutes of the meetings that the scheme of amalgamation was unanimously approved in the said meetings held on 18-12-2018 approving the scheme of amalgamation.

27. On a query by this Court as to whether the meetings were attended and held by the shareholders and creditors 'majority in number representing three-fourths in value', it was shown to this Court by referring to the various annexures that despite sending notices of the EGM of the petitioner companies (i) by registered posts, (ii) by circulating the resolutions of the companies as to approaching this Court in the websites of the DSE and CSE, (iii) by exhibiting the news of proposed amalgamation in the screen of the DSE and CSE and (v) by publishing in the two daily newspapers, while a significant number of shareholders together with the 90% of the creditors of the transferee company attended the meeting and unanimously voted in favour of the arrangement of amalgamation, the meetings of shareholders and creditors of the transferor company were held in presence of 100% of all the stakeholders and wholeheartedly supported the scheme. Thus, it appears that although the arrangement of amalgamation in question was voted by the overwhelming majority of the creditors and members of the transferor company having satisfied the requirement of `majority in number representing three-fourths in value' as stipulated in section 228 of the Companies Act, the transferee company's meeting (EGM) apparently was not attended by the 'majority in number representing three-fourths in value' albeit the 90% creditors attended the meeting (EGM) and extended their full support to go ahead with the scheme of amalgamation. Against the above backdrop, the question comes up for consideration of this Court as to whether the proposed scheme of amalgamation deserves this Court's approval. In other words, whether non-attendance of majority shareholders of one of the two companies in the meetings (EGMs) held for obtaining vote of the shareholders for amalgamation would be an impediment for this Court to grant sanction to the proposed scheme of amalgamation.

28. The unambiguous wordings 'majority in number representing three-fourths in value' employed in section 228 of the Companies Act dictates this Court that in order to make an arrangement binding upon the shareholders, creditors, company and all other concerns, there are two conditions; firstly, the said arrangement must be made with the consents of more than fifty percent of the shareholders and/or creditors and, secondly, the shareholders and/or creditors who voted in favour of the arrangement must be the owners of three-fourths of shares and/or credits in value. From a careful reading of the different provisions regarding 'meeting and proceeding' as provided in sections 81 to 88 of the Companies Act, it appears that the procedures for calling, holding and conducting the Annual General Meeting (AGM), Statutory Meeting, Extra-ordinary General Meeting (EGM) and Board Meeting are different from the procedures of a meeting to be called, held and conducted under section 228 of the Companies Act at the instance of the Company Court. Also, the requirements of a resolution for arrangement under section 228 of the Companies Act are quite different from the requirements of extraordinary or special resolution under section 87 of the Companies Act. Thus, mere unanimous majority votes of the presentees would not be sufficient for adopting a resolution under section 228 of the Companies Act.

29. Having held as above, I find that while the transferor company fully satisfies the criterions of section 228 of the Companies Act, the transferee company strives to fulfill the legal requirement. Under the circumstances, this Court has two options, namely (i) either to direct the transferee company to call and hold a fresh meeting of the shareholders to ensure the presence of majority shareholders, or (ii) to dismiss this application. If this Court now directs the transferee company to call and hold a meeting for the second time and ultimately the number of presentees becomes the same, it would be a futile exercise of power of this Court. And, if this Court dismisses the application on the ground of non-fulfillment of the aforesaid criteria, the transferee company inevitably shall go for a fresh meeting with its shareholders with an expectation of seeing a gathering of more than fifty percent of the shareholders. But if the transferee company is met with the same experience, what would be the ultimate fate of the petitioner-companies. In the aforesaid' scenario, then, a legitimate question crops up as to whether this Court is powerless to remedy the citizen when the Court will find that the concerned citizen has put in his best efforts to comply with the laws and who is not at fault. In my considered view, since the Legislature never intends to make a law to see its application impossible in practice, and since the Company Court randomly applies the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, (shortly, the CPC), thus, the inherent power under section 151 of the CPC together with the inherent power vested in this Court by the provision of Rule 263 of the Companies Rules, 2009 (Companies Rules) may be invoked to deal with this kind of situation towards doing justice. The above view was taken by this Court in the case of Kay and Que vs RJSC 2019(2) 16 ALR 32 (relevant Para-43) in according approval to the petitioner-companies for amalgamation. The aforesaid inherent power under section 151 of the CPC read with Rule 263 of the Companies Rules being a discretionary power in nature, the Court must apply the same in the most fit and deserving cases where the Court will find the efforts of the petitioner to be bonafide and the ultimate decision shall not affect the public at large. In the case in hand, the transferee company apparently has put in its best efforts to ensure the presence of the general shareholders in the meeting called at the instance of this Court's direction by sending the notice of the said meeting (i) by registered post, (ii) by displaying the notice in the TV scroll, (iii) by exhibiting the news of amalgamation in the electronic screen of the DSE and CSE, (iv) by circulating the news in the web-portals of the DSE and CSE and (v) by publishing the advertisement in two daily newspapers and, therefore, this Court finds the petitioner companies' efforts as to ensuring the majority attendance in the meeting to be bonafide towards compliance of the legal requirements under section 228 of the Companies Act.

30. The above analysis of the facts in reference to the relevant statutory laws and case-laws leads me to hold that the petitioner companies have succeeded to satisfy this Court as to the requirements under section 228 of the Companies Act.

31. Now, let me take up the issue No. 2, namely, whether the petitioner-companies have been in breach of any laws of the land in preparation of the scheme of amalgamation. It has been alleged by the learned Advocate for the BSEC that since the transferor company is ineligible to go for Initial Public Offer (IPO), it has cunningly invoked the provisions of sections 228 and 229 of the Companies Act. From a bare reading of the relevant provisions of Bangladesh Securities and Exchange (Public Issue) Rules, 2015, in particular Rules 3(3)(a) and 14(d), it appears to this Court that a company desirous to be enlisted through IPO requires to comply with 469 requirements, including 3 (three) years valuation report of securities. Apparently, it is a rigorous process for a company to get enlisted through IPO. However, the liquidation of shares through IPO and transfer of shares through amalgamation being regulated by the two completely different laws, there is hardly any scope for this Court to entangle the petitioner-companies' present move of amalgamation with the breach of laws governing IPO. The second allegation raised by the BSEC is that the petitioner-companies have employed a CA Firm in violation of Rules 12(2) and 12(38) of the Securities and Exchange Rules, 1987 (hereinafter referred to as SE Rules). Upon perusal of the above laws, it appears that every company is bound to submit annual report prepared by a `credible' CA Firm following international accounting standards, so that it reflects the true financial affairs of the company. The petitioner-companies have employed ACNABIN to carry out their audits for the purpose of the proposed amalgamation, and it is the contention of the BSEC that since there is allegation of professional misconduct against the ACNABIN which awaits receiving a verdict from the ICAB, the regulatory body of the Chartered Accountants, its report should not be accepted by the Court. Given that the allegation in question against the ACNABIN is pending before the Chartered Accountants' regulator) body 'Institute of Chartered Accountants of Bangladesh' (ICAB), albeit without subjecting it to any interim prohibitive order in carrying out its professional work, it would be fair for ACNABIN if it withdraws itself from any work when it would be encountered with the above-mentioned issue, inasmuch as the law requires credible audit report from a CA Firm; and until and unless ACNABIN gets discharged of the accusation brought against it, credibility of its works to the general people would be questionable. Since it is an admitted position that an investigation against the ACNABIN's one of the partners is currently undergoing and since ACNABIN's appointment has been alleged to have been a violation of the Rules 12(2) and 12(3B) of the SE, Rules, this Court, in order to remain transparent, ordered the petitioner-companies to carry out their audit for the purpose of ascertaining the fair valuation of their shares on the basis of NAV and EPS of the last two financial years (2017-2018 & 2018 to 2019) by engaging Nurul Faruk Hasan & Co. which is affiliated with one of the Big-4 CA Firm, named, Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited (hereinafter referred to as the "Deloitte").

32. Issue No. 3 is whether the petitioner-companies' audit reports were prepared in consonance with the Guidelines of the International Accounting Standard (IAS). It has been alleged that in preparing the audit report, ACNABIN used the tactics of increasing the value of shares of the transferor company by revaluing its assets from 323 crore to 978 crore and by not revaluing the assets of the transferee company.

33. Let me deal with the aforesaid contention/allegations. While there is no law in Bangladesh that sets any standard or technical requirement for valuation with respect to amalgamation, IAS 1 (Para 31, 34), IAS 16 and IFRS 13 require assets of a company to be presented at fair value, not at historical costs, and permits revaluation of assets. 1AS 16, Para 31 provides that "after recognition of an asset, an item of property, plant and equipment whose fair value can be measured reliably shall be carried at a revalued amount, being its fair value at the date of the revaluation less any subsequent accumulated depreciation and subsequent accumulated impairment losses. Revaluation shall be made with sufficient regularity to ensure that carrying amount does not differ materially from that which would be determined using fair value at the end of the reporting period".

IAS 16, Para 34 provides that,

"... some items of property, plant and equipment experience significant and volatile changes in fair value, thus necessitating annual revaluation. Such frequent revaluations are unnecessary for items of property, plant and equipment with only insignificant changes in fair value. Instead, it may be necessary to revalue the item only every three or five years."

34. From the above-quoted provisions of the International Accounting Standard (1AS), it appears that revaluation of asset of any incorporated company is a permitted exercise. However, the objections raised by the BSEC are, firstly, about selection of only transferor company for revaluation; had both the petitioner-companies' assets been revalued by the auditor ACNABIN, the BSEC could not have raised any objection. Secondly, the basis for calculating PIE ratio (Price to earning ratio) used by the ACNABIN is against the global standard of valuation, because it has used its own PIE multiple for the transferee company, which is a listed company. It has been contended by the learned Advocate for the Deloitte that the globally accepted and established practice is to compute a Benchmark EPS multiple based on listed-comparable companies operating in the same jurisdiction (peer set). Thirdly, it is evident that ACNAB1N did not take into consideration the BSRM's EPS of the Financial Year 2019 in computing the P/E ratio of BSRM. The learned Advocate for the Deloitte Ms Farhana Khan points out that because of ACNABIN's omission in computing the BSRM's EPS of FY-19, there was fundamental effect on lowering BSRM Ltd.'s share value. It has been professed by the learned Advocate for the Deloitte that the EPS of FY-19 being the most recent one, it reflects the most latest financial position of BSRM, and had ACNABIN used EPS of FY-19 to calculate P/E multiple, keeping all other data set same (i.e. average of 6 month's price of BSRM LTD, earning of 5 years' net profit after tax weighted based on outstanding shares), value per share of BSRM LTD would have been Taka 61.89 and, on the other hand, had ACNABIN used EPS of FY-19 to calculate P/E multiples, average of 1 year's price of BSRM LTD, earning of 2 years' net profit after tax and weighted based on year of earning, value per share of BSRM LTD would have been Taka 91.83.

35. On 19-10-2020, the Court-appointed CA Firm Deloitte submitted its report to this Court wherein the NAV of the transferee company is recorded at Taka 97.46 and the EPS is recorded at Taka 114.74 and, thereby, Deloitte determined the price of per share for the transferee company at Taka 108.98. And, for the transferor company, the Deloitte found the NAV per share at Taka 34.57 while as per EPS multiple method, the value per share of transferor company was assessed at Taka 29.88. It means that while there is no change in terms of NAV calculation of the transferor and transferee company by ACNABIN and Deloitte respectively, Deloitte found higher share price for transferee company under the EPS multiple method. 36. While the learned Advocate for the BSEC accepted Deloitte's valuation with some observations, Mr Tanjib-ul Alam along with Mr Imran Anwar, the learned Advocates for the petitioners, raised objection to the calculation of share price under the EPS multiple method for the transferee company done by Deloitte on the following three grounds; (i) there is no basis for determination of the share price under the EPS multiple method because there is no explanation on how the P/E multiple of 12.50x was arrived at for the transferee company and P/E multiple of 10.75x was arrived at for the transferor company; (ii) there is no basis for accepting 66.67% weight for the EPS multiple approach compared to 33.33% weight for the NAV approach of share valuation and (iii) there is no calculation of the EPS.

37. In reply to the objection raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioner-companies, the learned Advocate for the Court-appointed auditor, Ms. Farhana Khan professes that EPS multiples are the measurements or expressions of EPS method in practice and it is one of the methods used in Market Value Approach. In elaborating her reply, she makes the following points; that EPS refers to earnings per share of a company, computed as reported Profit After Tax for an accounting/fiscal year divided by the outstanding number of shares of the company; that once EPS is determined, in order to derive valuation of the shares, the multiples need to be computed; that the multiples can be equity based multiples like Price to Earnings (PIE), Price to Book Value of Equity (P/B), Price to Sales (P/S) etc; that the most popular and widely used equity based multiple is earnings multiple; that as the Court directed valuation based on Earning Per Share (EPS), which is basically valuation based on earning multiple (Price to Earnings (P/E) multiple), Deloitte has conducted valuation following the Order of the Court; that EPS multiple is calculated through EPS Multiple, which is synonymous. to Earnings Based Valuation or Price to Earnings multiple method, computed as Price per Share divided by Earnings per Share; that since computation of fair value of shares of BSRM LTD and BSRM SML is on independent but on relative basis, for determining value of shares of each company, it was important to use a consistent approach to arrive at the EPS multiple to be applied to the EPS of respective companies; that this was to ensure that in determining share exchange ratio of each company on the basis of the relative value of shares of each company, various factors having a bearing on the share valuation, including the operational history, growth, profitability, liquidity of shares, etc. are accounted for and adequately reflected in the share valuation; that for valuing shares applying EPS methods, the subject entity's (i.e. BSRM LTD and BSML) EPS (earning or profit per share) is multiplied with applicable P/E multiple; that this is the method that have been applied by both Deloitte and ACNABIN; that EPS based valuation, EPS multiple based valuation, P/E multiple based valuation, earning multiple based valuation, EBV (Earning Based Valuation) - all are essentially different terms for the same thing; that Deloitte has used the term 'EPS Multiple Method' - to correspond with the method name with the Court's Order; that while both Deloitte and ACNABIN have adopted similar methodology, the conclusions differed as a result of basis for calculating P/E ratio or the Price to Earning Multiples between the two valuers; that as per global standards of valuation, using own P/E multiple for a listed company (here for BSRM LTD) in a relative valuation of two entities is not generally accepted practice; rather the globally established practice, as adopted by Deloitte, is to compute a Benchmark EPS multiple based on listed, comparable companies operating in Bangladesh ("Peer Set"), excluding one of the subject companies - "BSRM LTD" in this Peer Set, and applying the Benchmark EPS multiple to both of the entities.

38. Thus, this Court finds that while on the one hand, the petitioner-companies failed to apply their due diligence in appointing a competent audit firm for preparation of their scheme of amalgamation in terms of the provisions of Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (Public Issue) Rules, 2015, on the other hand, their auditor failed to apply the globally accepted norms and practice in carrying out their audit works in line with the principles/guidelines of lAS.

39. Let me now embark upon the issue No. 4, namely, whether the Company Court is competent to intervene in the audit report prepared by a CA Firm. The Company Court has been vested ample power by section 229(f) of the Companies Act to pass any Order/Direction in effectively adjudicating upon the amalgamation cases. However, normally, the Company Court is reluctant to interfere with the auditor's report in course of dealing with a scheme of amalgamation and its valuation report unless it becomes incumbent upon the Court to meddle in it towards protecting the interest of general people or any other class on the ground of ex-facie unfairness and violation of provision of any law. Moreover, when the credibility of a CA Firm would be attacked by a party of the relevant case with reference to a specific occurrence of professional misconduct, the provisions of the Security Exchange Rules in tandem with the principles of natural justice demand that the Court of law shall intervene in the matter to mitigate the situation by appointing another reputed CA Firm without making any adverse comment about it till the period the allegation pending against CA Firm is disposed of by their regulating body. In approving a scheme of amalgamation, in an appropriate case, this Court shall not shrug off its duty to ensure that interests of the particular class of shareholders are not adversely affected while another class secures undue benefits out of such merger and, thus, the Company Court would not merely play the role of a rubber stamp. Accordingly, in this case, another CA Firm Nurul Faruk Hasan & Co was appointed by this Court, and that too was done as per the recommendation of the learned Advocate for the petitioner-companies.

40. In Hindustan Lever Employees' Union vs Hindustan Level Limited, (1994) 4 Comp L.1 267 (SC), in Paragraph 43, the Supreme Court of India cited with approval the passage from Takeovers and Mergers by Weinberg and Blank, where it stated that in amalgamation of two companies, some or all of the following factors will have to be taken into account in determining the final share exchange ratio: (i) The Stock Exchange prices of the shares of the two companies before the commencement of negotiations or the announcement of the bid. (ii) The dividends presently paid on the shares of the two companies. It is often difficult to induce a shareholder, particularly an institution, to agree to a merger or a share-for-share bid if it involves a reduction in his dividend income. (iii) The relative growth prospects of the two companies. (iv) The cover (ratio of after-tax earnings to dividends paid during the year) for the present dividends of the two companies. The fact that the dividend of one company is better covered than that of the other is a factor which will have to be compensated for at least to some extent. (v) In the case of equity shares, the relative gearing of the shares of the two companies. The 'gearing' of an ordinary share is the ratio of borrowings to the equity capital. (vi) The values of the net assets of the two companies. Where the transaction is a thorough-going merger, this may be mere of a talking-point-than a matter of substance, since what is relevant is the relative values of the two undertakings as going concerns. (vii) The voting strength in the merged enterprise of the shareholders of the two companies. (viii) The past history of the prices of the shares of the two companies. In Maftalal vs Maftalal Industries Ltd., 2000 ECR 19 (SC), while the Supreme Court of India cautioned that valuation of shares is a technical and complex issue, which can be appropriately left to the consideration of experts in the field of accountancy 'Paragraph 39', in GL Sultani vs The Securities and Exchange Board of India, AIR 2007 SC 2172, the Supreme Court of India acknowledged that since valuation involves subjective and objective assessment of various factors, there is considerable scope for difference of opinion amongst the experts, even applying correct principles. Mathematical precision and exactitude are not the attributes of share valuations, for at best the valuation arrived at by an expert is only his opinion as to what the value of the share should be (Paragraph 37).

41. It leads me to hold that when a proposed merger is manifestly unfair or is being proposed unfairly, or unfair or contrary to public policy, this Court is well competent to protect the interest of such shareholders whose interests have not been properly protected in the scheme.

42. Another submission that has been advanced by the learned Advocates for the petitioners in reference to the FEID Circular No.-1 dated 06 May 2018 issued by Bangladesh Bank that the market price/quoted price as prevalent in the stock exchanges are the fair price for shares of the transferee company because this is the price against which the shares are currently traded in the market and which the shareholders of the transferor company is willing to pay for the transferee company and, accordingly, the closing market price of transferee company, being 57.4, should be the fair price. He, however, offers Taka 69.45 to be the fair price which has been calculated by ACNABIN Chartered Accountants considering conservative approach in calculating EPS and NAV, by which the general shareholders will have no reason to be aggrieved but, according to him, the valuation done by Deloitte being sky-high, it would be unreasonable to ask the shareholders of the transferor company to pay significantly higher price than what the investors can otherwise buy from the stock market at market price. Mr Alam has referred to a plethora of cases in a bid to show this Court that the quoted price/market price for a listed entity is the fair price to pay in a merger. The cases include; (i) Commissioner of Wealth Tax vs Mahadeo Jalan and Mahabir Prasad Jalan, AIR 1973 SC 1023, (ii) Mafatlal Industries Ltd. [1995] 84 Comp Case 230(Guj), (iii) the case of Coimbatore Cotton Mills Ltd. and Lakshmi Mills Co. Ltd., [1980] 50 Comp Case 623 and some other cases.

43. On this point, the learned Advocate for the Court-appointed auditor professes that in valuing a listed company, it is not imperative that the market price of such company should be used as the only method, because Guidelines for Foreign Exchange Transactions (GFET), 2018 Vol 1 issued by Bangladesh Bank, Chapter 9, section - I, Para 3(A) states that in situations where repatriation of funds against transfer of shares of listed companies are involved, Bangladesh Bank would not require a separate valuation for listed companies if the sale proceeds do not exceed market price; that it imposes a ceiling or the maximum amount that can be repatriated against such share transfer without independent or separate valuation, by reference to market price of publicly traded shares, in an effort to regulate outward remittances from Bangladesh; that by no means it would appear to be a prescriptive Guidelines from Bangladesh Bank, imposing an obligation on publicly listed companies to value their shares only at quoted market price; that the provisions of Bangladesh Bank 2018 Guidelines essentially refers to whether valuation is required or not in case of transfer of shares and remittance of sales proceeds of non-residents' investment in a listed company in Bangladesh; that this does not change the definition, approach and methodology of valuation; that is actually issued pursuant to Paragraph 3(B), Chapter 9 of the Guidelines for Foreign Exchange Transactions-2018 (GFET) Volume 1, stipulating various instructions on how to perform valuation of shares with details of the approaches and methodologies when non-resident share transfers are involved; that though the valuation methods prescribed by Bangladesh Bank in FEID Circular No.- 1 of 06 May 2018, do not have direct applicability when valuation of shares in mergers of two local companies are concerned, the valuation methodology contained therein are formulated in accordance with the globally accepted practice, which are certainly useful parameters in assessing the accuracy of a valuation method adopted by a valuer; that in the Market Value Approach prescribed by Bangladesh Bank, it is performed using comparable company trading multiples; that Bangladesh Bank has also directed that in Market Values Approach based valuation, market value should be average of one year month-end-average values of companies of peer group, as opposed to 6 months' valuation; that the quoted price on the market was not adopted even in that valuation report, inasmuch as the market price of BSRM Ltd.'s shares on valuation date 30 June 2019 was Taka 70.90, rather than Taka 41.44 as derived by ACNABIN under Market Approach.

44. It is the view of this Court that when a non-listed company's share is going to be merged into a listed company, calculation of share exchange ratio on the basis of quoted price of the listed company's share solely—is not only against the existing accounting policy, but also is incompatible with common sense. Because if the value of the share of the transferee company is determined on the basis of the quoted price, the share price of the transferor company also should be fixed on the basis of its quoted price, but there being no quoted price of the shares of the transferor company, there is no scope of application of the said proposition/principle. And, even if the transferor and transferee companies, both, are listed companies, it is the auditor who would be the sole and final arbiter to decide whether market price of the shares of the transferor and transferee companies would be the basis of calculation of the share exchange ratio or not. Because, while in the normal scenario quoted price in a Stock Exchange would be a safe and proper basis for fixing the share exchange ratio, however, for the most volatile share markets, such as Bangladesh's share market, it may not be a wise decision for an honest, prudent and experienced CA Firm to rely on the quoted price.

45. 1 have gone through the cases referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner-companies in an effort to persuade this Court for accepting the quoted price of the transferee company, and it appears to me that the contexts in which the cited ratio were laid down are quite different from the factual backgrounds of this case and, more importantly, the legal provisions regulating the merger/amalgamation issues in India are dissimilar from that of our country in that the Indian law requires a scheme of amalgamation to be first vetted and approved by their regulatory body 'Security and Exchange Board of India', but in our law there is no such legal device in place. Therefore, this Court does not find the ratio of the case laws referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner-companies to be applicable here in the case in hand. Moreover, while the Courts of most of the jurisdictions professed general non-interference with the valuation and scheme of amalgamation, the Indian Supreme Court in Maftalal vs Maftalal Industries Ltd., 2000 ECR 19 (SC) in interpreting section 391 of the Indian Companies Act, 1956. with which section 228 of our Companies Act shares its legacy, after reviewing strings of Indian and US case laws, including the Indian Supreme Court's stance in Hindustan Lever Employees' Union vs Hindustan Level Limited, [1994] 4 Comp LI 267 (SC), postulated that no Court of law would ever countenance any scheme of compromise or arrangement arrived at between the parties and which might be supported by the requisite majority, if the Court finds that it is an unconscionable or an illegal scheme or is otherwise unfair or unjust to the class of shareholders for whom it is meant.

46. Now, let me examine the Fifth issue, namely, whether the proposed scheme of amalgamation would imperil general share-holders' interest. It is the apprehension of the BSEC that burden of a huge amount of Taka 2788 crore loan of the transferor company will go upon the shoulders of the 59.06% general shareholders and, secondly, it has been alleged that after amalgamation since the transferee company's sponsor shareholders will hold 76.09% shares, if they sell 46.09% shares, keeping the 30% shares, there is every possibility that the prevailing market share price will be diluted significantly. It is contended by the learned Advocate for the Deloitte that if the valuation of shares and the share exchange ratio submitted with the scheme of amalgamation is adopted, it will result in greater dilution of shareholding by the public shareholders, whereby the public shareholding percentage in BSRM Ltd. would be reduced to 23.91%, whereas as per the Deloitte's valuation, percentage of public shares would be 27.59%; that while the dilution of public shareholding would be inevitable as a result of the proposed merger, if the Valuation Report of scheme of amalgamation, and consequent share exchange ratio, is sanctioned by the Court, the eventual increased rate of dilution would mean reduced dividends for the public shareholders while the sponsors would enjoy increased dividend; that the possibility of reduction in dividend is particularly significant in view of the fact that in 2019, BSRM Ltd. had declared dividend @ 25%; that though the scheme of amalgamation has been shown to have been approved by the majority shareholders, the public shareholders have not been duly consulted inasmuch as no reasonable and honest man, who is a member of public shareholding class, and acting alone in respect of his interest as such a member, would approve of this scheme of amalgamation limiting his scope of dividend earnings in the future.

47. Regarding the BSEC's concern as to the Bank liability of the transferor company, I have meticulously examined the appended papers and it appears to me that while the Banks of the transferor and transferee companies are happy about the collateral and have extended their full support towards amalgamation, there is hardly any reason for others to be worried. And, regarding the general shareholder's risk of losing the market price if the sponsor shareholders sell out their shares in the market, this Court expressed its mind at the very outset of hearing this case that after amalgamation of any public listed company with non-listed company, there shall be a lock-in period of 3(three) years for the persons who are sponsor shareholders and Directors who were/are in the Boards of the transferor and transferee-companies and, by doing it, it is hoped that the risk of losing money by the general shareholders will be lesser inasmuch as the general shareholders shall have ample time either to retain the shares or to dispose of the same at their convenience.

48. Relying on the papers, documents submitted by the petitioner-companies as well as on the submissions made by this learned Advocate Mr Tanjib-ul Alam which was augmented by his junior Mr Imran Anwar, that the scheme of the amalgamation has been undertaken for the purpose of economical benefit of both the companies, their shareholders, employees and other stakeholders; that the scheme of amalgamation would ensure to achieve their business objectives as well as to conduct their business more efficiently and profitably; that the purpose of the amalgamation is to keep pace with the present competitive market and to strengthen the position of the companies; that since nearly half of the shares of these two companies are being held by the same set of persons, hence, there is no malafides on their parts to cause harm to the ultimate company; that there is no question of being prejudiced by any third party; on the other, since it is the findings of this Court that there is no objection from the creditors, shareholders and employees and, further, since this Court is convinced that the interest of all the shareholders and creditors will remain protected by the revised `share exchange ratio' and 'the lock-in period', this Court is of the view that the proposed scheme of amalgamation may be approved by this Court with the exchange ratio as assessed and determined by the Court appointed CA Firm Nurul Faruk Hasan & Co (Deloitte).

49. Accordingly, the scheme of amalgamation (Annexure-A to this petition, except the share exchange ratio, which shall be 1:0.288), as approved at the respective EGMs of Bangladesh Steel Re-Rolling Mills Limited, and BSRM Steel Mills Limited, held on 18-12-2019, as set out in annexures-U Series, from the effective date of the scheme of amalgamation, is sanctioned by this Court. Hence it is ordered that-

(1) The transferor-company and transferee-company be amalgamated in terms of the scheme of amalgamation, annexed as Annexure-A, except making one change therein with regard to share exchange ratio, fixing the same to be 1:0.288. As per the aforesaid ratio, the public/general shareholders' percentage shall be recorded 27.59%. The scheme of amalgamation, in the revised form as per this Court's Order, shall form part of this Judgment and Order.

(2) The sponsor shareholders and all the past and present Directors of the transferor and the transferee companies are restrained from selling, gifting or transferring the shares of the ultimate company (transferee company) in any manner till expiry of 3 (three) years from the effective date of amalgamation. (3) The Judgment and Order shall take effect after filing of the certified copy of the same to the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firm by the transferee-company and subject to annexing copy of this Judgment and Order to every Memorandum of the transferee-company issued after this Order is passed.

(4) It is further ordered that all the pending suits and proceedings, if any, henceforth shall be commenced and be continued by or against the transferee-company, as the case may be, as if the same are to be or have been filed by or against the transferee-company.

(5) It is also ordered that the whole undertaking, properties and liabilities of the transferor-company shall be vested in and transferred to the transferee-company, subject to the compliance of the terms and conditions of the said scheme of amalgamation.

(6) It is also ordered that all the shares, debenture, policies, license and other like interest in the said transferor-company be transferred to and vested in, appropriated and allotted to the transferee-company in terms of the said scheme of amalgamation.

(7) It is also ordered that all mortgages, charges, undertakings, assurances obligation, liabilities, if any, of the said transferor-company shall be transferred to and vested in, be taken by and be enforceable by or against the transferee-company in the same manner and to the same extent as if all of these acts, deeds and things have been done by the transferee-company.

(8) Upon this amalgamation coming into effect, as per sub-section (1)(d) of section 229 of the Companies Act, the transferor-company shall stand dissolved without winding up and the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms is hereby directed not to register any company in the name and style of the aforesaid transferor-company.

(9) Since, by virtue of this Judgment and Order, all the assets and liabilities of the transferor-company have been transferred to and vested in the transferee-company, so all the liabilities of the said transferor-company (if any) shall become the liabilities of the transferee-company and if the properties of the transferor-company is encumbered, in any manner, the same shall continue and the properties of the transferor-company shall be transferred to and be vested in the transferee-company subject to such encumbrance and charges, if any, to the transferee-company.

(10) Upon amalgamation, the experiences and qualifications of the transferor-company shall be treated as the experiences and qualifications of the merged entity.

(11) Upon amalgamation, the accounts of the companies be finalized and circulated amongst the members of the said transferor-company and the transferee-company.

(12) It is further directed that all regulatory bodies and Government Authorities, including Registrar of Joint Stock Companies & Firms, the National Board of Revenue, Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Ltd, Sub-Registrar of the concerned area as well as lending institutions, including Banks and Leasing companies shall give effect to this scheme of amalgamation without any further act, petition or order whatsoever. Registrations, Certificates, Agreements and/or Deeds including Property Deeds shall be deemed to have been transferred from the said transferor-company, namely, BSRM Steel Mills Limited to the transferee-company, namely, Bangladesh Steel Re-Rolling Mills Limited from the effective date.

(13) This Judgment and Order shall not affect the personal guarantee or similar other obligations, if any, of the directors, shareholders and third-party guarantors of the transferor-company.

(14) It is also ordered that transferee-company shall cause certified copy of this Judgment and Order to be delivered to the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms, for registration within 14 days as required by sub-section (3) of section 229 of the Companies Act, from the date of receiving certified copy of this Judgment and Order.

(15) The entire costs in respect of the scheme of amalgamation shall be borne out by the transferee-company, namely, Bangladesh Steel Re-Rolling Mills Limited.
